# Contagion by invisible living agents (germ theory) (`contagion_theory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by microscope, microorganisms, spontaneous_generation_refuted, natural_causes
- Core idea: Many diseases are caused by living things too small to see, which multiply in the body and pass to the next person by specific routes: excrement in water and food, unwashed hands, coughing, wounds, and biting insects (fleas, lice, mosquitoes). Different agents may cause similar illnesses, and some have several routes, so the defence differs: clean water against cholera, delousing against typhus, clean hands against childbed fever. Not bad air (miasma), not the stars, not an imbalance of humours. The most convincing argument without a microscope is practical: block one route and compare deaths between exposed and less-exposed groups or before and after an intervention (Semmelweis's two wards, Snow's two water companies). Koch's historical criteria for causal evidence were: find the germ in every case, grow it pure, produce the disease with it in an animal, and recover it again. Some infections do not meet all these criteria.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming all diseases are caused by germs (scurvy, rickets, pellagra, goitre, cancer and many others are not)
  - Saying 'tiny animals cause disease' without naming the route, so nobody knows what to do differently
  - Assuming every disease spreads through the air or by touch; bubonic plague, malaria and epidemic typhus commonly involve insect vectors, while pneumonic plague can spread between people, cholera needs swallowed excrement
  - Dismissing miasma measures entirely: draining swamps and removing filth did work, for the wrong reason
  - Believing that seeing microbes proves they cause disease; healthy people are full of harmless ones
- History: rome: c. 37 BC – Varro warns of invisible tiny animals from marshes entering through mouth and nose (De re rustica I.12); a guess with no consequences; islamic: c. 1349–1362 – Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Khatima (Granada) argue from observation that plague passes by contact, clothes and vessels; china: 1642 – Wu Youxing, Wenyi lun, says epidemics come from specific pestilential agents entering by mouth and nose, not from weather; europe: 1546 – Fracastoro, seeds of contagion; 1835 Bassi shows a fungus causes a silkworm disease; 1840 Henle; 1860s Pasteur; 1876 Koch proves anthrax, 1882 tuberculosis; Koch's postulates stated 1884–1890
- Read:
  - Girolamo Fracastoro, De contagione et contagiosis morbis et eorum curatione (1546)
  - Robert Koch, Die Aetiologie der Tuberculose, Berliner klinische Wochenschrift (1882)
  - Paul de Kruif, Microbe Hunters (1926)
